issues.title: Out-of-range mixed-moment indices

failure_location.quote: for all nontrivial subsets $C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of cardinality at most $k-1$

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims a condition for every nonempty C contained in {1,...,n}, but z is defined only as (z_1,...,z_k). Whenever n>k, an allowed C may contain an index greater than k, so the product over i in C is undefined. The same malformed contract is subsequently used by prop:distributionexistence.
issues.overall_effect: The distributional hypothesis of prop:momentmatch and the existence claim in prop:distributionexistence are not well-defined in the intended n>k regime.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In both eq:specialdistrib and prop:distributionexistence, replace the ambient index set C contained in {1,...,n} by C contained in {1,...,k}, while retaining the bound |C|≤k−1 and retaining n in the binomial coefficient on the right-hand side. The example and existence proof then apply unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The vector z has exactly k coordinates, and the example and existence proof organize the conditions solely by moment orders 1 through k−1. Thus {1,...,k} is uniquely forced by the old source; {1,...,n} is a copied out-of-range index, and its correction changes no inference or guarantee.

issues.title: Infeasible quick-decay assumption
issues.failure_explanation: The old condition asserts R(s)=s+epsilon for every s in [t,1], with epsilon positive. Necessarily R(1)=1, so no well-defined ratio can satisfy the condition at the required endpoint. Away from the endpoint, the positive additive offset can support a lower comparison but not the analogous upper relative comparison claimed in eq:approxexpect.
issues.overall_effect: The printed kernel hypothesis has no admissible instance for positive epsilon, making prop:momentmatch vacuous as an applicability result, while its proof does not establish the stated upper moment bound from the one-sided condition.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Let R_pi(s) denote the displayed integral ratio. Replace R_pi(s)=s+epsilon by the two-sided relative condition (1−epsilon)s≤R_pi(s)≤(1+epsilon)s, equivalently |R_pi(s)/s−1|≤epsilon, for all relevant s in [t,1]. Substituting s=1/z in the existing walk calculation then supplies both sides of eq:approxexpect. Merely imposing |R_pi(s)−s|<epsilon would not preserve the same relative-error conclusion without changing its tolerance.
issues.why_classification: The old premise is infeasible because R_pi(1)=1, and its one-sided additive offset does not justify the proof's upper relative bound. This is therefore not transcriptional. Nevertheless, one local, source-supported correction of the kernel premise makes the same walk-sum proof work with the same conclusion, error rate, and intended fast-decay regime, without a new lemma or proof architecture.

issues.title: Dimensionally invalid sampling construction

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we denote by $U[a,b]$ the uniform distribution on the interval $[a,b]$

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition quantifies over arbitrary d and requires a kernel whose two arguments lie in R^d, but it defines x_i and y_j using scalar interval distributions. For every admissible d>1, the resulting kernel evaluations used to define A and B are therefore outside the declared domain.
issues.overall_effect: As written, prop:momentmatch does not define its sampled kernel matrices in dimensions greater than one, so its claimed multidimensional expected-moment bound is not established.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define each x_i as a vector uniformly distributed on [0,1]^d and, conditional on z_j, define y_j=z_j^(−1/d)u_j with u_j uniform on [0,1]^d. Rewrite the proof's l-point integration domains and change-of-variables map over l blocks of d coordinates; when s denotes a volume fraction, the scaled numerator domain is ([0,s^(1/d)]^d)^l. The resulting density factor is the product of the relevant z_j values, equal to z_1^l under the stated almost-sure equality condition, so the existing moment calculation and multidimensional conclusion are preserved.
issues.why_classification: The kernel domain, the dth-root scaling, and the multidimensional examples clearly support the vector-cube construction. However, the correction must also be propagated through the scalar integration domains and change-of-variables calculation, so it requires genuine mathematical checking rather than a single transcriptional reading. That propagation is a routine local vectorization and needs no new lemma, construction, or weakening of the dimensional guarantee.

issues.title: Inconsistent experimental dimension
issues.failure_explanation: The experiment constructs its kernel matrices from samples whose stated dimension is six, while the declared kernel has domain R^7 x R^7. Consequently, the kernel evaluations needed to form A and B are undefined under the printed setup.
issues.overall_effect: The third numerical experiment is not executable or reproducible as stated, although the theoretical formal results are not affected by this local experimental inconsistency.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use one ambient dimension consistently throughout the experiment. A complete local route is to retain the stated d=6, change the kernel declaration to kappa:R^6×R^6→R, use six-dimensional samples for both matrices, and verify the plotted data against that setup, regenerating the figure if necessary.
issues.why_classification: Making the kernel and samples dimensionally consistent is local and leaves all theoretical results untouched. It is not safely classed as a typo because the source alone does not establish whether six- or seven-dimensional data generated the existing figure; a routine verification or rerun is needed. No nontrivial mathematics or meaningful empirical guarantee is lost.

issues.title: Contradictory trial count

failure_location.quote: Two averages over $m=8000$ runs of finding $B$ are shown, illustrating the variation inherent to our framework.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We perform $m=128000$ trials of forming $B=(Y,Y)$ and average the $j$th largest eigenvalue thus obtained for $1\leq j\leq k$.

issues.failure_explanation: The caption claims that each displayed average was formed from 8000 runs, while the old example's procedure specifies 128000 trials for forming and averaging B. The factor-of-16 discrepancy leaves the reported empirical sample size internally inconsistent and prevents an unambiguous reconstruction of the experiment.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical evidence in the third example has an ambiguous trial count and is not exactly reproducible from the text, but no formal theorem or theoretical dependency is affected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Adopt the procedure's m=128000 count consistently: verify that both displayed averages used 128000 runs, or rerun them with that count if necessary, and replace m=8000 in the caption by m=128000.
issues.why_classification: Neither conflicting count is uniquely forced as the count underlying the existing figure, so this is not a pure typo. Resolving it requires only a local data check or routine rerun and a caption correction; the illustrative empirical claim remains comparable, and no formal result or theoretical guarantee is affected.
